offence_severity: Minimum: Life imprisonment, Maximum: Not specified
physical_harm: Severe fracture and injuries resulting in profuse bleeding and eventual death
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence on record, particularly the testimonies of eye-witnesses - PW-7, PW-8 and PW-9 are consistent, trustworthy and fully corroborates with one another, without giving any room to doubt their credibility. Their evidence is also fully supported by the testimony of PW-10 and PW-11. All the facts directly point to the guilt of accused No.1. The testimony of PW-1 is fully corroborated with medical evidence.
witness_credibility: The evidence of the main witnesses is consistent, trustworthy and fully corroborates with one another, without giving any room to doubt their credibility. The testimony of PW-1 is fully corroborated with medical evidence.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 5th July, 1997; Trial judgment: 15th December, 1998; High Court decision: 16th June, 2006; Supreme Court decision: 2nd July, 2014
legal_representation: Krutin R. Joshi, Gunashekar, Rajesh Mahale, Advs. for the Appellant; V. N. Raghupathy, Lagnesh Mishra, Parikshit Angadi, Sanjay R. Hegde, Advs, for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Acquittal; High Court: Conviction under Section 302 IPC; Supreme Court: Dismissed the appeal, upheld the High Court's conviction
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused, Pundappa Yankappa Pujari, was involved in the assault that led to the death of Mahantappa, and that the evidence of the eye-witnesses and medical evidence supported the conviction under Section 302 IPC.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the Trial Court's acquittal was reasonable and that the Appellate Court should not have reversed the order of acquittal without sufficient grounds to doubt the credibility of the eye-witnesses.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that if two views are reasonably possible from the same evidence, the Appellate Court cannot impose its own view unless it is satisfied that the Trial Court's view was wholly unreasonable or perverse.
precedent_relied_upon: Hem Raj and another v. State of Punjab [2003) 3 Suppl. SCR 466; T. Subramanian v. State of Tamil Nadu [2006) 1 SCR 180; Haji Khan v. State of U.P (2005) 13 SCC 353
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the act of the accused resulted in the death of the deceased, and it fell within the ingredients of Section 300 IPC, making it punishable under Section 302 IPC.
